title: Time-Integrated Leakage as a Dynamical Benchmark for Multi-Mode Superconducting-Qubit Reset
abstract: Reset performance in superconducting qubits is often summarized by the population that remains at the end of the pulse. This is an important number, but it does not describe what happens during the reset itself. A protocol may reach a small final residual while keeping the qubit in a leakage state for a comparatively long part of the trajectory. In this work, we therefore use time-integrated leakage, together with the usual endpoint population, to study a multi-mode dissipative reset model under flux-frequency control. We examine finite thermal occupation, parameter sweeps, frequency disorder, an auxiliary-chain ablation, and a literature-based rate benchmark. At the representative ablation point, adding the auxiliary chain reduces Lf from 8.56 to 0.78 ns and shifts the sustained Pf less-than- 10-2 crossing from 39.5 to 9.8 ns. Interestingly, the configuration without the chain still reaches the smaller long-time residual. The two metrics can therefore favor different reset configurations. For the same 300 ns analysis window, an effective rate model built from the f-ket and e-ket decay rates reported by Zhou et al. gives Lf is 108.0 ns, while the complete simulated configuration gives 0.783 ns. We use this only as a kinetic reference and not as a reproduction of the experiment. In the wider set of simulations, thermal occupation is the main source of degradation, while the frequency disorder considered here has a much weaker effect. The results suggest that time-integrated leakage is a useful quantity to report alongside endpoint residuals, especially when reset is part of repeated quantum-error-correction cycles.
summary: This work introduces time-integrated leakage as a necessary metric for evaluating superconducting-qubit reset protocols, arguing that final residual population alone is insufficient. By simulating a complex multi-mode system, the authors demonstrate that transient leakage can reveal performance limitations missed by endpoint measurements. This is vital knowledge for designing robust quantum error correction cycles.
main_problem: The paper addresses the limitation of using only the final residual population to characterize superconducting-qubit reset performance, proposing time-integrated leakage as a superior metric.
main_result: Time-integrated leakage ($L_f$) is a crucial diagnostic tool, as it can reveal performance bottlenecks missed by endpoint measurements, especially when comparing different reset protocols.
method: The authors use numerical simulations solving the master equation for a multi-mode superconducting qubit system under flux control and dissipation.
model_or_system: The system is a superconducting transmon qubit coupled to a multi-mode auxiliary chain and a lossy resonator, modeled using a Lindblad master equation approach.
key_observables: Time-integrated leakage ($L_f$), final residual populations ($P_f(t_f)$), and sustained threshold times ($t_s(\epsilon)$).
important_parameters: Thermal occupation ($ ar{n}$), frequency disorder ($\Delta$), and the coupling strength of the auxiliary chain.
main_assumptions: The dissipative model is effective and not fully device-calibrated; the comparison to literature rate models is explicitly noted as a kinetic reference only.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the qubit architecture, and subsequent figures show trends of residual leakage and population versus disorder strength or thermal occupation.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem by comparing metrics, details the multi-mode dissipative model, presents ablation studies comparing different circuit components, and concludes by advocating for the use of time-integrated leakage in error correction contexts.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous, quantitative framework for analyzing open quantum system dynamics in superconducting circuits, moving beyond simple steady-state measurements to characterize the entire reset trajectory.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Figure 1: Architecture studied in this work. Time-dependent flux modulation shifts the transmon frequency, the coupled auxiliary-mode chain provides distributed dissipative pathways, and the lossy resonator supplies an additional excitation-removal channel.
Figure 2: Distribution of residual leakage across the thermal-noise simulations. The broad upper tail reflects thermal re-excitation away from the lowest-residual operating regime.
Figure 3: Residual population versus integrated leakage. Point color denotes filter thermal occupation and point size denotes final ground- state population.
Figure 5: Residual population as a function of resonator loss for two representative filter thermal occupations.
Figure 4: Residual leakage versus filter thermal occupation. The monotonic trend indicates that filter thermal photons dominate the variation across the sampled thermal-noise data.
